title: The super Keyword
summary: Master the super keyword for constructor chaining, accessing shadowed fields, and calling overridden methods.
learningObjectives: Understand the role of the super keyword as a direct reference to the parent class
Use super(...) to invoke parent class constructors with proper arguments
Understand the strict rule: super(...) must be the first statement in a constructor
Use super.fieldName to resolve shadowed or hidden parent fields
Use super.methodName() to call and extend parent methods from an overridden child method
expectedOutcomes: Complete mastery over all three uses of the super keyword in Java
Ability to write clean constructor chaining and method extensions without compiler errors

activities.title: The Parent's Workshop Analogy
activities.content:
Imagine you are an apprentice carpenter working in your parent's workshop.

You have your own personal toolbox (`this`), but right next to you is your parent's master toolbox (`super`).

Sometimes, you and your parent have tools with the exact same name, like a hammer. If you simply shout "Hand me the hammer!", your assistant grabs your personal hammer (`this.hammer`). But if you need your parent's heavy sledgehammer from the master rack, you say: *"Hand me the parent hammer!"* (`super.hammer`).

Furthermore, when building any furniture, your parent must first lay the master wooden foundation (`super()`) before you can carve your own decorative trim!

In Java, the **`super`** keyword is your direct bridge to your immediate parent class.

activities.title: The super Keyword: Reaching Into the Parent Class
Invoking Parent Constructors with super(...)
activities.description: See how a child class passes arguments up to initialize parent fields using super(...).

steps.description: Employee defines a parameterized constructor requiring name and basicSalary.
Developer constructor calls super(name, basicSalary) as its very first statement.
The Employee constructor executes first, setting up name and basicSalary.
The Developer constructor then completes, assigning primaryLanguage.

activities.title: Resolving Shadowed Fields and Calling Overridden Methods
activities.description: Observe super.field and super.method() in action when names overlap.

steps.description: Vehicle declares maxSpeed = 100 and a displayInfo() method.
SportsCar declares maxSpeed = 260, shadowing Vehicle's maxSpeed.
Inside SportsCar.displayInfo(), super.displayInfo() executes the parent method.
super.maxSpeed reaches through the shadow to print the parent's 100.

activities.codeSnippet:
super.displayInfo(); // Calls parent method
System.out.println(super.maxSpeed); // Reaches shadowed parent field

activities.title: Quick Check: The super Keyword (10 Questions)

questions.question: What is the primary role of the super keyword in Java?
options: To refer directly to the immediate parent class (superclass)
To make a class run on multiple CPUs
questions.explanation: The super keyword is a reference variable pointing to the immediate superclass.

questions.question: Where must the call to super(...) be placed in a child constructor?
options: As the very first statement in the constructor
At the very end of the constructor
questions.explanation: Java strictly mandates that super(...) must be the very first statement in a constructor.

questions.question: What happens if a child class defines a variable with the same name as a variable in the parent class?
options: The child field shadows (hides) the parent field
The parent field is deleted from memory
Both fields are merged together into an array
questions.explanation: This is field shadowing. The child field hides the parent field within the child's scope.

questions.question: How can a child class access a parent field that has been shadowed by a child field?
questions.explanation: super.fieldName explicitly references the field in the immediate superclass.

questions.question: Can a constructor contain both a this(...) call and a super(...) call?
options: No, because both this(...) and super(...) must be the first statement
Yes, if separated by a semicolon
questions.explanation: Both calls require being the first statement, making it impossible to have both in the same constructor.

questions.question: Can you write 'super.super.method()' to call a grandparent's method in Java?
options: Yes, you can chain as many super references as needed
No, Java explicitly disallows 'super.super' to preserve encapsulation
Only if the grandparent is abstract
questions.explanation: Java forbids 'super.super'. You can only reference members of your immediate parent.

questions.question: If a child overrides void save(), how can it call the parent's original save() method?
questions.explanation: super.save() invokes the superclass implementation of the overridden method.

questions.question: Can the super keyword be used inside a static method?
options: Yes, to access static superclass methods
No, super cannot be used in a static context because static methods belong to classes, not instances
Only if the method is synchronized
questions.explanation: Just like 'this', 'super' cannot be used in static methods because it relies on an object instance.

questions.question: What happens if a child constructor does NOT explicitly call super(...) or this(...)?
options: The compiler automatically inserts an invisible, no-argument super() call as the first statement
The parent constructor is completely skipped
questions.explanation: The compiler automatically inserts 'super()' to initialize the parent with its default constructor.

questions.question: If parent class has only 'public Parent(int x)' and no no-argument constructor, what happens if child does not call super(x)?
options: Compilation error: constructor Parent in class Parent cannot be applied to given types
It runs but crashes at runtime
questions.explanation: The compiler tries to insert super(), but since no no-arg constructor exists in Parent, compilation fails.

interviewQA.question: What are the three distinct usages of the super keyword in Java?
interviewQA.answer:
1. Invoking superclass constructors: 'super(...)' to pass parameters to the parent constructor.
2. Accessing shadowed superclass fields: 'super.fieldName' when child declares a field with the same name.
3. Invoking overridden superclass methods: 'super.methodName()' to execute parent logic before or after child behavior.

interviewQA.question: Why does Java enforce that super() must be the very first statement in a constructor?
interviewQA.answer: Java enforces the first statement rule to guarantee deterministic object initialization. A subclass instance is built upon the foundation of its superclass. If child statements could run before super(), the child might read or modify uninitialized parent state, leading to subtle bugs or undefined behavior.

interviewQA.question: Can this() and super() be used together in the same constructor?
interviewQA.answer: No. Both this() (constructor chaining within the same class) and super() (chaining to the parent constructor) must be the first statement in a constructor body. Since a constructor can have only one first statement, they cannot coexist in the same constructor. However, this() eventually delegates to a constructor that invokes super().

interviewQA.question: What is the difference between super and this in terms of memory and binding?
interviewQA.answer: 'this' is an explicit object reference pointing to the current instance, subject to dynamic virtual method dispatch. 'super' is a keyword that tells the compiler to bypass the current class's virtual table entry and directly dispatch to the immediate superclass implementation.

interviewQA.question: Can super be used in a static method or static initialization block?
interviewQA.answer: No. The super keyword represents an instance reference to the superclass. Static methods and static blocks belong to the class level and operate without any object instance; therefore, referencing 'super' in a static context results in a compilation error ('non-static variable super cannot be referenced from a static context').

interviewQA.question: What happens if a superclass does not define a no-argument constructor?
interviewQA.answer: If a superclass defines parameterized constructors and no zero-argument constructor, the compiler cannot automatically insert an implicit 'super()' call. Any subclass constructor MUST explicitly invoke one of the available parameterized parent constructors using 'super(args)'; otherwise, a compile-time error occurs.

activities.title: 10-Point Mastery Checklist: The super Keyword
checklist: I can name all three usages of the super keyword
I know how to call a parent constructor using super(...)
I understand why super(...) must be the very first statement
I know how to resolve shadowed fields using super.fieldName
I know how to invoke parent methods using super.methodName()
I understand why super cannot be used in static methods
I know that this() and super() cannot be placed in the same constructor
I know that Java automatically inserts implicit super() if omitted
I know what compile error occurs when parent lacks a no-arg constructor
I understand the difference between this and super

practiceProblems.title: Constructor Chaining with super(...)
practiceProblems.problemStatement:
Create a parent class `Book` with a constructor `public Book(String title, double price)` initializing fields `String title` and `double price`.
Create a child class `Textbook` extending `Book` with an additional field `String subject`.
Write a constructor `public Textbook(String title, double price, String subject)` that calls `super(title, price)` as its first statement.
Add a method `void showDetails()` printing `title + " (" + subject + ") - $" + price`.
In `Main.main()`, instantiate `Textbook("Linear Algebra", 89.99, "Mathematics")` and call `showDetails()`.
hints: In Textbook constructor, 'super(title, price);' must be the first statement.
Assign this.subject on the line below super.

practiceProblems.title: Shadowed Field Resolution From Scratch
practiceProblems.problemStatement:
Write a complete program from scratch demonstrating shadowed field resolution:
1. Parent class `Shape` with field `String type = "Generic Shape"`.
2. Child class `Circle` extending `Shape` with field `String type = "Round Circle"`.
3. Add a method `void displayBothTypes()` inside `Circle` that prints:
   `"Child type: " + type`
   `"Parent type: " + super.type`
4. In `Main.main()`, instantiate `Circle` and invoke `displayBothTypes()`.
practiceProblems.expectedOutput:
Child type: Round Circle
Parent type: Generic Shape
hints: 'super.type' accesses the shadowed field in Shape.

practiceProblems.title: Extending Parent Logic with super.method()
practiceProblems.problemStatement:
Create:
1. Parent class `Logger` with method `public void log(String msg)` printing `"[BASE LOG] " + msg`
2. Child class `TimestampLogger` extending `Logger` that overrides `log(String msg)`.
   Inside the overridden method, call `super.log(msg)` first, and then print `"[TIMESTAMP] 12:00:00 UTC"`
In `Main.main()`, instantiate `TimestampLogger` and invoke `log("System update complete.")`.
hints: Call super.log(msg) inside TimestampLogger's log method.
Follow it with the timestamp print statement.

practiceProblems.title: Bug Hunt: Constructor super() Placement Violation
practiceProblems.problemStatement: The following program fails compilation because `super(...)` was placed after a print statement. Fix the constructor order so the program compiles and produces the expected output.
practiceProblems.expectedOutput:
Constructing Dog...
Rover the Beagle barks!
hints: Move 'super(name);' to be the first line inside the Dog constructor.
The print statement can follow super(name).

practiceProblems.title: Tiered Transaction Fee Processor
practiceProblems.problemStatement:
Build a financial transaction fee engine:
1. Parent class `Transaction`:
   - `protected double amount`
   - Constructor `public Transaction(double amount)`
   - Method `public double calculateFee()` returning `amount * 0.02` (2% fee)
2. Child class `InternationalTransaction` extending `Transaction`:
   - `private double foreignExchangeFee`
   - Constructor `public InternationalTransaction(double amount, double fxFee)` calling `super(amount)`
   - Override `calculateFee()` to return `super.calculateFee() + foreignExchangeFee`
   - Method `public void printSummary()` printing `"Total fee: $" + calculateFee() + " on transaction of $" + amount`
In `Main.main()`, test `InternationalTransaction(1000.0, 15.0)` and call `printSummary()`.
hints: calculateFee() in InternationalTransaction calls super.calculateFee() (which computes $20.0) and adds foreignExchangeFee ($15.0) = $35.0.
